transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman.
Stocks opened mixed this morning as anthropic shares gave up some of their early trading gains.
NPR's Scott Horsley reports the Dow Jones industrial average rose more than 400 points in early trading.
Anthropic shares opened down as early investors pocketed some of their gains from the previous day.
Stock and the company that built the popular AI chatbot Claude jumped 17 percent on their first day of trading Thursday,
even as the broader market fell.
The Trump administration has auctioned off leases for underwater mining on millions of acres of seabed near American Samoa.
The first-of-its-kind auction went forward this week despite legal objections from critics
who say there hasn't been enough study of the potential environmental damage.
And gasoline prices continue to fall. AAA says the average price of regular gas tipped to $3.69 a gallon just ahead of the busy Thanksgiving travel week.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
A group of Senate Democrats wants to block funding for the Iran war through a must-pass bill next month.
NPR's Claudia Grisales reports some worry it could lead to a government shutdown.
Virginia Democratic Senator Tim Kaine wants to include a provision that would block money for the Iran war in a must-pass government funding measure.
He argues since President Trump did not seek congressional authorization, the war is illegal and Congress should not fund it.
If you want to keep waging war against Iran, there is a path to do it.
Come and seek a congressional authorization, which they should have done from the first day.
Democrats' votes are needed to pass a government stopgap measure in the Republican-led Senate,
so some hope to use that leverage now to stop the war.
However, there's concerns among Democrats that it could lead to a government shutdown if they don't reach a deal with Republicans by a December 11th deadline.
Claudia Grisales, NPR News.
The incoming chair of the House Judiciary Committee is investigating how Homeland Security and Justice Department officials preserve communications when they're doing official business.
Democrat Jamie Raskin has sent letters warning that he is concerned the Trump administration is using apps that self-delete after a period of time.
Raskin says that would violate laws about governmental recordkeeping. He's demanding the agencies take steps to recover any deletions.
The U.S. Army says that it has delayed today's controlled detonation of thousands of pounds of bomb-making material in southeastern Iowa.
It's been moved until Monday.
Many people in Iowa and some in neighboring Illinois did not know about this detonation until this week.
The U.S. Army says it is worried the material is unstable and could go off by itself.
But some groups sued the EPA.
They alleged any detonation will release a toxic cloud that could spread and harm nearby residents.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
The White House has named a new National Cyber Director. Kirsten Davies has been serving as the Pentagon's Chief Information Officer.
She'll take over from Sean Cairncross.
This follows several high-profile tech issues recently, ranging from last week's grounding of airline traffic to bank and computer troubles.
A new study shows that six in 10 people who use A.I. for health advice say they would believe a chatbot even if it contradicted their health care provider.
NPR's Windsor Johnston reports on how those conversations are showing up in patient exam rooms.
Talker Research conducted the survey for the virtual care company MD Live.
Medical Director Dr. Maggie Williams says chatbots give quick, confident answers at any hour.
By the time patients come in, she says, many have already asked a chatbot about their symptoms.
That happens every day, multiple times a day.
And I think, honestly, many of our patients have conferred with CLOD or another resource and maybe don't even disclose it.
Williams says the risk goes both ways.
A chatbot could get someone to the ER sooner, but it can also suggest breathing exercises for chest pressure when someone's having a heart attack.
Windsor Johnston, NPR News.
Officials with the Cincinnati Zoo say that their beloved hippo, Fiona, has died.
She had recently eaten a visitor's hat.
Zookeepers had waited for nature to take its course, but there were complications.
After several attempts, zoo veterinarians were not able to help her.
This is NPR.
It's free through Amazon Music.
Or you can also support NPR's vital journalism and get NPR Plus at plus.npr.org.
That's plus.npr.org.

topics.text: Anthropic shares jump 17 percent on first trading day, then open lower
Trump administration auctions underwater mining leases near American Samoa despite legal objections
Gasoline prices fall, with regular averaging $3.69 a gallon before Thanksgiving travel
Senate Democrat Tim Kaine seeks to block Iran war funding in must-pass government funding bill
Jamie Raskin investigates Homeland Security and Justice apps that self-delete official communications
Army postpones controlled detonation of bomb-making material in southeastern Iowa until Monday
White House names Kirsten Davies as new National Cyber Director, succeeding Sean Cairncross
Survey finds six in 10 AI health-advice users would trust a chatbot over their provider
Cincinnati Zoo announces death of hippo Fiona after she ate a visitor's hat
